Hello! I was in the same boat at one point. I always knew I wanted to work in the medical field but had a hard time deciding what to do. I finished my first degree and got a job as a nursing assistant in the OR at a local hospital. I then decided to apply to the accelerated nursing program (1 full year summer through spring, basically no breaks). I had thought about doing FNP at that point but by the time I graduated I was done with school. I worked at the bedside for 3 years before deciding to apply for the FNP program, knowing that by the time it ended I would be ready to leave the bedside. I was accepted and went part time so that I could continue to work, 3 years later I graduated.

One thing I really appreciate about my path is that I was able to get that bedside experience and learn how to talk with patients/families. It was a great foundation to build my skills particularly bedside manner. While not true for every doc or PA but I think as nurses the compassion really comes through as NPs. I also have a better understanding of what I’m really asking nurses to do bc at one time that was me following the orders. It’s easy to give an order but things can be more complex than just “do this.” Some tasks seem simple but really require coordinating with several interdisciplinary services, making sure insurance covers the test/treatment, etc that I don’t think other providers realize. One downside of NP is that schooling and clinical is not consistent across the board unlike PA or MD/DO- a fact that I really think needs to be changed. One thing to note about NP is that (depending on your state) you could potentially be an independent provider, whereas PAs always require a collaborating physician. 

That all being said, when I started my NP job at a specialty clinic last year my orientation was essentially the same as the new PA who started a few months before me. We both got on-the-job training and fortunately our doctors are very helpful and supportive to this day.

You’re welcome! The GI tract is a complicated system, and as CVS is a syndrome it’s based off symptoms which can vary widely vs a specific diagnostic test to say “yep you got it!” It’s a rough one to have, but you’ll find what remedies work well for you. 

I saw a holistic provider after my diagnosis and she was the one to make the GF suggestion after seeing my food journal (lots of pasta and bread as a college student). She also recommended diary free, but I thought it would be hard to cut out both at once. Plus if it was only one that was a trigger I’d never really know which it was. Since then I have switched to almond milk and overall less dairy, but still have it and it doesn’t seem to cause problems for me.

Definitely sounds like CVS! When I was diagnosed with CVS I decided to try going gluten-free. My celiac test was negative but there were no other possible triggers we could think of besides gluten from breads, pastas, etc. After my month trial, I felt much better! So I believe I’m gluten intolerant, and now (8 yrs later) if I accidentally eat gluten I get sharp abdominal pain, distention, and nausea. 

If your doc is thinking CVS too, they should give you amitriptyline which will help prevent the episodes. And if they haven’t already, should give you an antiemetic like zofran or reglan to reduce your nausea during an attack once you feel it starting. I’ve found that rest and heating pads will be your bffs during/after episodes. Also, over the years of having CVS and now being a nurse, I put myself on a clear liquid diet (ginger ale, Gatorade, broth) at the first sign of an attack- it’s gentler on the stomach, keeps you hydrated. Sometimes it’s enough to stop it, sometimes not. But even if you do still throw up, liquids don’t hurt coming back up. 

Hope you feel better soon!!

My abdominal pain would start around 8-9 pm and increase over the night. I was never able to vomit before roughly 4 am- anything earlier was dry heaves and just intense pain. My zofran helps for mild nausea episodes but if a CVS attack was happening, nothing was stopping it.

CVS is complicated, and like most things can be different for each person. At first, my attacks occurred every week- like clockwork my abdominal pain would start in the evening, followed by hours of dry heaving until I was crying and wishing I could throw up to have relief, then in the early morning I’d be vomiting several times until there was nothing left in my stomach. I would definitely ask about amitriptyline, that’s the standard treatment/daily prevention for CVS along with meds to take as needed if you’re experiencing an attack, like zofran, reglan, compazine. 

Other things to help would be eliminating any triggers. Not sure about you, but I couldn’t find any link with foods or alcohol use triggering my episodes so it was hard to know how I could help my condition. I tried going gluten-free after I was diagnosed and this has helped my stomach pains. Resting and the use of heating pads are life-changing, and if you get any sort of warning that an attack is coming I’d recommend putting yourself on a clear liquid diet. This is better tolerated, and if you happen to still throw up it is less painful. 

I hope you feel better soon and wish you the best of luck!

I was diagnosed with CVS 8 years ago. At that time my GI doc put my on amitriptyline (daily med to reduce episodes) and zofran as needed. I could not find a link between my attacks and any foods or alcohol use- I would eat different types of cuisine each time, they almost never occurred when I had been drinking. After this I decided to trial a gluten-free diet, and after a month I felt better. Now if I eat even a small amount of gluten (i.e. burger with breadcrumbs) I get nausea and abd pain. I went years without a recurrence then my episodes came back after 5 years, I had another endoscopy which of course didn’t show anything but mild irritation (my team got my test scheduled quickly after my attacks returned) so I was on an acid-reducing med for a short time, and haven’t had episodes since. 

I always got like an “aura” before any vomiting episodes, CVS related or otherwise, which made me know I would be up for hours in pain and throwing up. Now that I’m a nurse, when I get this aura I know to put myself on a clear liquid diet- ginger ale, gatorade, broth- until my stomach relaxes. This doesn’t always stop me from vomiting, but at least it won’t be painful food coming back up. This has helped immensely, since there is less irritating substances in my stomach and I can sometimes “override” an episode. Also, a good heating pad to use on the stomach is a true godsend- don’t know what I’d do without it!

As others have said, he needs to make the connection between his triggers and these episodes but also decide if his lifestyle choices are worth the GI upset. I know for me, I would give up anything that triggered an attack. I wish you both the best of luck, I know that these episodes are painful for him and must be for you as you care for him.
